item.title: We're living in an AI twilight zone
item.description:
Two seemingly contradictory realities are true at once:

  1. Most people find AI only modestly useful, a more clever Google search.
  2. Many people building AI or using it obsessively worry it could severely damage or destroy humanity.

Why it matters: We're living in an AI twilight zone. For many, the technology is simultaneously underwhelming in daily use and terrifying in its trajectory.

  • The gap between these two realities helps explain why confusion and fear are exploding across politics, AI labs and business.

State of play: The AI labs are in full panic. They worry the public dislikes AI and despises data centers — and that's before Anthropic insiders went public with their latest warnings that AI could end humanity this decade.

  • They're uncertain how to showcase potential benefits of AI when X and now mainstream media are lit up with horror stories about rogue or ruinous AI.
  • The data center backlash showed how fast public opinion turned against them. Their worst-case scenario: They lose full control of the politics, with both parties rushing to slow or stop AI in the run-up to the election.

Between the lines: The past 36 hours show how fast politics and public opinion are moving. A low-level Anthropic employee for all of four months drove the national conversation — and 142 million views on X alone — by warning AI could end humanity.

  • Numerous people, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have issued similar warnings to us for years. But the tone and timing struck a nerve — and stirred countless members of Congress to call for new AI regulations.

Zoom in: Let's look at this tale of two worlds through two different sets of eyes — a mid-career manager and an Anthropic data scientist.

  • The average manager has limited time to experiment with AI, worries it might threaten their job, and mostly uses the models as a search engine and for writing better emails or presentations. It's a nice-to-have, sometimes delightful, other times unimpressive. They don't understand the hype.
  • The Anthropic employee spends all day, every day, staring at rapidly improving AI, often mesmerized, even spooked, by what it does. They see it exceeding even the most optimistic benchmarks, then spend their nights and weekends with similar AI obsessives discussing how it could cure cancer — or go rogue and destroy humankind. To them, this is truly civilizational and existential — a clear reality, not hype.

The catch: AI companies have to explain both realities at once. But almost every version of the pitch sounds suspicious.

  • Tell Americans today's AI will transform their lives, and many look at their own experience and wonder what the fuss is about.
  • Tell them tomorrow's AI could become vastly more powerful, and the obvious response is: Then why are you racing to build it?

Warn about catastrophic risk while spending hundreds of billions to accelerate development, and critics hear either hypocrisy or fear-based marketing.

  • But keep in mind that the big AI labs are working with unreleased models weeks before the public sees them — plus early training data on future models, months in advance. So they are often warning about progress invisible to the public and government.

The big picture: The politics are shifting fast. Until now, much of the AI backlash centered on tangible costs — lost jobs, deepfakes, power bills and data centers.

  • Then on Tuesday, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit and accused frontier labs of "gambling with our lives."
  • Anthropic's alignment-science lead — who still works at the lab — responded by agreeing that AI could kill humanity, and said his personal odds of that happening in the next decade are over 10%.

By Wednesday afternoon, the alarm had gone bipartisan in a Washington already rattled by OpenAI's Hugging Face incident:

  • Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) described AI companies as being in a "blind race to build a death machine first." Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) renewed his push for a bipartisan AI kill switch.
  • Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who has already proposed a data center moratorium and ban on superintelligence, is convening senators next week for a briefing on AI's "extraordinary dangers."
  • Rep. Don Beyer, a Democrat from Northern Virginia, tweeted: "I hope warnings like these will help my colleagues understand how important it is to take broad action on AI regulation, and to do it swiftly."
  • Even Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), one of Washington's loudest advocates for beating China in the AI race, called the risks "dangerous and frightening" and said guardrails are needed.

The bottom line: The AI twilight zone has created fertile ground for a generational populist backlash.

  • The industry requires Americans to absorb enormous disruption today for a future its own builders describe as miraculous or apocalyptic — sometimes in the same breath.

Axios' Zachary Basu contributed to this report.

item.title: Elon Musk's X is the AI community group chat
item.description:
Elon Musk bought Twitter saying civilization needed a "common digital town square." Four years later, it's more like a live group chat for Silicon Valley's AI obsessives.

Why it matters: Two years ago, X was fighting off competition from a slew of new entrants. Today, it remains relevant by becoming more niche.

  • The people making AI news are often debating it, explaining it and occasionally breaking it on X before the rest of the information ecosystem catches up.

State of play: New model releases, research papers, demos, hiring moves, high-profile executive exits and technical arguments ricochet through X in real time.

  • The latest viral example came Tuesday when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation on X, along with a thread explaining his safety concerns. The post has over 100 million views.
  • Another Anthropic employee chimed in to say he thinks there's a >10% chance that AI could kill all humans in the next decade.
  • The combination sparked a ferocious news cycle about the dangers of scaling AI, and it was all kicked off by two employees posting on X.

Flashback: The AI community, particularly the researchers who define the technical progress happening within frontier AI labs, has long coalesced around ideas on X.

  • Back in 2025, Anthropic AI researcher Andrej Karpathy coined the term "vibe coding" in an X post, helping name one of the defining trends of the AI enterprise adoption curve.
  • Even executives are now engaging more with the platform as a communications tool, with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang launching his account in July alongside a post supporting open AI models.
  • Researchers from Chinese AI labs are breaking geographic boundaries to reach new audiences on X, per Wired, which is part of what helped catapult open models to their current popularity.

Zoom in: Huge investments in live video have made X a go-to platform for new live tech shows, such as "TBPN," "Stabledash," "MTS Live" and others.

  • While those shows don't always have viewership numbers that rival cable TV or even content creators on other platforms, the audience of AI insiders they attract has high value.
  • Just ask TBPN: the network was acquired by OpenAI for a rumored "low hundreds of millions," according to The Financial Times.

Yes, but: AI buffs are still a tiny subset of X's overall user base, and data shows X faces ample competitive pressure from Threads in engaging the everyday user.

  • Meta's Threads had 141.5 million daily active mobile users as of January 2026, topping X's 125 million, per Similarweb data.

Reality check: Musk didn't create "AI Twitter." Researchers and tech industry figures were already an influential part of the network long before he arrived.

  • But Musk closed the Twitter acquisition just a month before OpenAI released ChatGPT.
  • That kicked off an AI race whose participants were already networked together on the platform.
  • Big Tech CEOs like Huang and Apple's new CEO John Ternus are now joining the platform to communicate major AI announcements. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg also returned to posting on X this year, after letting his account lay largely dormant since its creation in 2009.

Zoom out: X itself is becoming an AI product.

  • Musk's xAI acquired X, saying the companies would combine their data, models, computing power and distribution.
  • Grok, the AI model from xAI, can use a connected X account to read timelines and follow what's happening on the platform.

The bottom line: Under Musk, X has morphed into an AI obsessives group chat. That may not be relevant for the vast majority of the platform's users, but it is for some of the most powerful innovators in the world.

item.title: Scoop: Anthropic whistleblower gave up his equity to leave the company
item.description:
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit his job due to concerns about the safety of AI two months before his equity would have vested, he told Axios.

Why it matters: The disclosure raises the stakes on Coxon's now mega-viral resignation from the AI lab, which laid out the broad view that the tech could end humanity.

What they're saying: "I no longer have anything to gain by juicing up Anthropic's valuation... I left before any of my equity vested," Coxon said in an interview with Axios Wednesday.

  • In his post on X announcing his resignation, which now has over 115 million views, he wrote: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt."
  • Other AI researchers, particularly from Google, have resigned over safety. But they did so after years of work, and presumably after their stock vested.
  • Coxon was at Anthropic for just four months, and employees have to be there for six months for their stock to vest, he said. He still has equity in his prior employer, OpenAI.

The big picture: Anthropic has traditionally been viewed as more publicly cautious and safety-oriented than other frontier AI labs, making Coxon's departure particularly striking.

  • Coxon said he has not seen Anthropic compromise safety to outlast its competitors, but he is concerned about the future: "If you're under pressure to race, you have to cut corners" or "skip steps in the oversight process," he said.
  • Those concerns can sometimes go too far, he said, describing what "sometimes feels like there's maybe excessive paranoia of OpenAI, excessive paranoia of China" that can help justify pushing ahead.

Threat level: As AI models are getting better, faster, they're also becoming harder to monitor.

  • That, combined with the pressure to win on AI, was Coxon's breaking point that led him to quit.
  • What was once science fiction about models knowing they are being tested, for example, is now "just a daily fact of working with these AIs," he said.
  • "They know when they're being tested, and they will think about the fact that they're being tested."
  • "The word doom is kind of silly," he said, adding that serious leaders in the industry are "on record saying they ... expect the potential for human extinction."
  • The danger was evident during the many recent cyber incidents across frontier AI labs, he said.

The bottom line: Coxon is one of now several people who have seen AI's peak capabilities up close — and are warning that what they saw could end humanity as we know it.

item.title: AI's extinction debate breaks containment
item.description:
An online panic erupted this week after millions discovered that leading AI researchers routinely debate and calculate the risk of human extinction.

  • Taken at face value, the odds are chilling: 10%, 20%, sometimes far higher, assigned to the possibility of AI catastrophe.

Why it matters: An esoteric debate over "p(doom)" has suddenly become a gut-level question for lawmakers, investors and millions of ordinary people: Why are we racing toward a technology its own builders believe could destroy us?

Driving the news: A resignation post by Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher who previously worked at OpenAI, has drawn over 110 million views on X after he accused frontier labs of "gambling with our lives."

  • The warning became vastly more explosive when Evan Hubinger, who leads Anthropic's Alignment Science team, publicly backed Coxon — saying "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans."
  • Hubinger said that, in his view, the odds of human extinction within the next decade are over 10%, and that Anthropic still has no plan for how to keep superintelligence under human control.

The big picture: Hubinger's post was widely cast as either a nightmare communications gaffe or a calculated dose of fear marketing from Anthropic, weeks before an IPO that could value the company at $2 trillion.

  • In reality, his position has been echoed for years by AI's most influential figures: Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-winning "godfather of AI," has estimated a 10%–20% chance that AI causes human extinction.
  • Elon Musk has put the risk as high as 20%. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told Axios last year that there's a 25% chance things go "really, really badly."

What they fear: "Doom" is a catch-all for several paths to catastrophe, from bad actors weaponizing powerful AI to advanced systems slipping beyond human control.

  • Humans with superpowers: AI could sharply lower the barrier to designing biological weapons, launching devastating cyberattacks or crippling critical infrastructure.
  • Machines with agency: A sufficiently autonomous system could deceive its overseers, copy itself, evade safeguards and resist attempts to shut it down.
  • The nightmare scenario: AI begins improving AI faster than humans can understand or contain the process, eventually producing systems too capable for their creators to control.

Zoom out: The world underlying those p(doom) estimates has changed dramatically in just a year, as frontier AI has made breathtaking leaps in autonomy, cyber capability and its ability to accelerate AI research itself.

  • Paul Christiano, the former OpenAI alignment chief who joined its board and safety committee Wednesday, said he shares safety fears about AI entering a rapid cycle of self-improvement.
  • "If we build superintelligence without more robust alignment I expect we will permanently lose control of it," Christiano wrote. "If that happens then most people could die."

Between the lines: AI researchers speak a probabilistic dialect that sounds utterly foreign to most normal people.

  • Inside a lab, a 10% p(doom) can be shorthand for enormous uncertainty about unprecedented technology. In ordinary life, almost nobody would tolerate that risk from a plane, a drug or a nuclear reactor.
  • Imagine Boeing's head of safety telling you before takeoff that there's a one-in-10 chance the next generation of aircraft ends in catastrophe — and that Boeing still doesn't know how to make it safe.

What to watch: That is increasingly how the warnings are being heard outside the labs — as a safety alarm, rather than a probabilistic thought experiment.

  • In Washington, the alarm is slowly intensifying: Sen. Bernie Sanders has proposed a ban on superintelligence and is convening senators for a briefing next week on AI's "extraordinary dangers."
  • The bigger political risk is that Americans were already souring on AI over jobs, power bills and data centers long before extinction entered the mainstream conversation.

item.title: Energy Department raises 2027 diesel price outlook by 33 cents amid Iran war
item.description:
The Energy Department's statistics arm on Wednesday sharply raised its forecast for U.S. diesel prices next year as tight global supplies keep domestic inventories unusually low.

Why it matters: The outlook suggests Americans could face elevated fuel costs well into 2027, as President Trump acknowledged Wednesday that oil prices may not fall until after November's midterm elections.

  • U.S. diesel prices hit all-time highs this month, due to the Middle East conflict thwarting oil and petroleum product supplies, and Ukraine's drone campaign targeting Russian refineries.

Driving the news: The latest Energy Information Administration outlook expects retail diesel to average $4.40 a gallon in 2027, up 33 cents, or 8.2%, from its previous forecast of $4.07.

  • The outlook says low U.S. distillate inventories are being driven by supply losses from the Middle East, Russia and China, alongside unusually high U.S. net exports.
  • It expects the inventory problem to be particularly acute this fall and winter because refinery maintenance cuts production just as agricultural and winter demand rises.
  • EIA also raised its 2026 forecast 22 cents to $5.07 a gallon.

Zoom in: "We forecast U.S. distillate fuel oil inventories will drop below 100 million barrels in September and will remain below the five-year (2021–2025) low through much of 2027," per the agency's statement.

  • "Tightness in the global distillate market has raised domestic prices and incentivized U.S. exporters to increase distillate exports," it added.
  • "We assume global production of distillate fuel will remain below last year's levels in the coming months, contributing to low U.S. diesel inventories and high diesel prices."
  • Representatives for the Energy Department and EIA did not immediately respond to Axios' Wednesday afternoon request for comment.

The big picture: Trump said Wednesday that oil prices would start "tumbling downward" after the election, but added that relief could take "a little bit longer than the midterms."

  • "I think for gasoline, we'll get them below $2 a gallon. But not until after the midterms," Trump said.
  • The comments mark a shift from Trump's prediction earlier this week that oil prices would fall "precipitously" after the U.S. wins the Iran war and that the decline would happen "quickly."

Zoom out: Before the Iran war, EIA expected diesel to average $3.47 a gallon in 2027 — 93 cents less than its latest forecast.

Caveat: EIA updates the outlook monthly, and its forecasts are subject to frequent revision as market conditions and underlying assumptions change.

Flashback: Trump repeatedly pledged during the 2024 campaign to cut U.S. energy prices in half within 12 months of taking office.

  • In March this year, Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNN, "We have seen a dramatic decline in gasoline prices, in diesel prices."

The intrigue: EIA expects diesel crack spreads — a measure of refining margins based on the difference between crude oil and diesel prices — to fall steadily through mid-2027 even as its forecast for retail diesel prices next year has risen.

  • That's based partly on an assumed return to normal tanker traffic through Hormuz in the near term, which would allow Saudi and Kuwaiti refineries to export more distillate.
  • EIA expects improved crude availability to East Asian refiners to boost distillate production.

Yes, but: If Middle East flows remain constrained beyond the end of 2026, EIA says global distillate crack spreads would be higher than currently forecast.

  • Russian refinery outages are expected to affect global markets through the first half of 2027.

What's next: The U.S. average retail diesel price could top $6 per gallon within the next week or so, GasBuddy's Patrick De Haan said Tuesday.

Go deeper: Iran war drives $100 billion in extra energy costs for U.S. consumers

  • EIA also raised its 2026 forecast 22 cents to $5.07 a gallon.

  • That's based partly on an assumed return to normal tanker traffic through Hormuz in the near term, which would allow Saudi and Kuwaiti refineries to export more distillate.
  • EIA expects improved crude availability to East Asian refiners to boost distillate production.

Yes, but: If Middle East flows remain constrained beyond the end of 2026, EIA says global distillate crack spreads would be higher than currently forecast.

item.title: Here's how AI could kill us all (if the worst fears come true)
item.description:
AI researchers shook the world Tuesday when they publicly acknowledged that there's a non-zero chance of AI killing off humanity in the next decade.

Why it matters: AI doomsday fears have existed for years, but as the technology has become more powerful and embedded in our lives, those warnings are breaking into the mainstream.

State of play: Anthropic researchers are sounding the alarm that rogue versions of superintelligent AI could destroy humanity.

  • Anthropic's Jacob Coxon wrote on X: "No other human activity poses this level of danger."

So how would AI kill us all, exactly?

Experts generally worry about two broad paths to catastrophe: humans weaponizing extremely powerful AI, or humans losing control of it.

  • In these scenarios, AI could make it easier for bad actors to create biological, chemical or other weapons.
  • Or rogue systems could attack infrastructure at unprecedented scale while evading human oversight.
Data: MIT IT FutureTech and the University of Queensland; Chart: Herb Scribner/Axios

How it works: In theory, a powerful rogue AI could evade oversight, replicate itself and resist attempts to shut it down.

  • This rogue AI could, in theory, develop biological or chemical weapons for nefarious actors, commit a massive cyber attack that cripples humanity's infrastructure, or centralize power in a way that would bring down civilization.

Another feared pathway is through recursive self-improvement, in which an AI helps build supercharged versions of itself before humans can understand it.

  • If this theoretical AI was misaligned from human goals, it could limit humanity's chances of containing or monitoring it before it acts out against humans.
  • OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Axios that models are developing quicker than humans can anticipate: "These models are getting superhuman in many of their capabilities, and we are just sailing in unknown waters."

Reality check: There's no scientific way to determine the odds of AI killing off humanity.

  • But insiders usually express their estimates using a shorthand — p(doom).

What is p(doom) exactly?

The term p(doom) is shorthand for a best guess at the probability that AI causes an existential catastrophe or doomsday scenario.

  • Many AI leaders and researchers believe p(doom) becomes increasingly more likely with the arrival of artificial general intelligence (AGI), the forerunner to superintelligence.

Context: "Doom" is in the eye of the beholder.

  • Some mean literal human extinction. Others include civilization's collapse or humanity's loss of control over society.

What are the odds of p(doom)?

The chances of p(doom) really depend on who you ask.

  • Roman Yampolskiy, an AI safety scientist, has put the chances at 99.99%.
  • AMI Labs founder Yann LeCun says any guess is a wild one, but p(doom) is "a lot less likely than a nuclear Holocaust."
  • Other estimates are similarly scattered: Elon Musk has put his p(doom) around 20%, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has estimated a 10%-25% chance of a catastrophic outcome.

More recently, AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton put the number at between 10%-20%.

  • Hinton told CNN: "Anybody who estimates probabilities like that is really just making a wild guess. They're just giving you their gut feeling."

Is doomsday possible yet?

We're not there yet. Experts generally agree that Claude, Grok and ChatGPT aren't plotting to end the world.

  • The 2026 International AI Safety Report, for example, said today's systems aren't capable of causing humanity to lose control.

AI would have to get much better at long-term autonomous planning, hiding its actions, evading oversight, gaining access to real-world systems and resisting shutdown attempts.

  • However, there are recent examples of AI agents acting autonomously and maliciously, beyond human understanding, resembling the type of rogue AI agents that some fear could lead to doomsday.

Can p(doom) be prevented?

Researchers are working on ways to lower the risk.

  • One such way is for humans to build kill switches or safeguards that could stop rogue AI agents.
  • A RAND report last April outlined nine mitigation strategies to stop bad actors from using AI to create deadly bioweapons, including more controls and safeguards.

Yes, but: This gets tricky, fast.

  • Leading AI companies are under pressure from shareholders, investors and their bosses to build, build, build — fast. The IPO headwinds could add to those incentives.
  • And it doesn't help that China and other U.S. AI companies are building their own powerful models, some open-weight and available for free, providing a potential runway for bad actors.

The bottom line: No one can accurately guess the odds of an AI doomsday, but scientists are sounding the alarm that the chances are real.

item.title: Anthropic insiders warn AI could kill all humans
item.description:
Three Anthropic researchers went public last night with chilling concerns about out-of-control AI, warning it could destroy humans this decade.

  • Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon wrote on X, after resigning Tuesday to sound the alarm: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible - but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger."
  • Anthropic alignment-science lead Evan Hubinger responded: "Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to."
  • Samuel Marks, Anthropic scalable-oversight lead, added: "AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes). This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are."

Why it matters: They're hardly alone. Their warnings came just days after top OpenAI leaders, including CEO Sam Altman, said AI is speeding into a scary, uncontrollable phase.

Via X

Warnings from inside the AI giants point to an epic shared dilemma: Slow down and risk falling behind, or press ahead and risk losing control. The companies are full speed ahead, even as they practically beg for regulation or a global pause, Axios' Maria Curi, Madison Mills and Ina Fried report.

The big picture: Calling this unprecedented would be a gross understatement. You basically have the fastest-growing companies in human history warning their products could harm or even destroy humanity.

  • Critics say Anthropic and OpenAI are hyping their products to raise their valuations and invite regulation that would benefit them alone as the dominant incumbents. But we've been talking with dozens of people inside these companies for months, and they've sounded increasingly spooked and concerned. Given they see models not yet released to the public, it seems reckless not to take them seriously.

🏛️ Context for readers from Mike & Jim: This is self-evidently scary stuff — and these vague warnings are impossible to validate or appraise. But we think readers, especially members of Congress and those in relevant federal agencies, need to be aware that the AI creators themselves see potential catastrophic outcomes absent a shift in how America, China and others review and release more powerful AI models.

💡 How to think about this: Nobody is warning AI is an imminent high-level threat. What they're saying is that the technology keeps improving faster than they thought possible and will soon be able to self-improve (recursive self-improvement). Once that happens, it gets even better, faster ... and much harder to predict or control.

  • Go deeper.

item.title: Medicare drug coverage faces an ominous spending outlook
item.description:
There are troubling new signs that the overhaul of Medicare drug coverage in the Inflation Reduction Act is dramatically driving up program spending.

Why it matters: The upward trajectory could threaten some seniors' coverage for outpatient prescription drugs — and it could force painful tradeoffs over the next decade as Medicare consumes a growing share of the nation's debt.

Follow the money: The IRA limited what seniors have to pay for outpatient drugs and shifted the remaining cost to taxpayers, insurers who provide stand-alone Medicare drug plans and drug manufacturers.

  • That was good news for enrollees who take expensive drugs for conditions like cancer, multiple sclerosis or rheumatoid arthritis and faced potentially crushing out-of-pocket costs.
  • But federal data shows demand for drugs is surging as they become more affordable, exceeding congressional scorekeepers' spending estimates and setting off more alarms.

Driving the news: Last week, congressional Medicare advisers reported that more than 1 in 5 enrollees hit Medicare Part D's $2,000 patient cost cap in 2025 — shifting new costs to the government.

  • 66% of total program drug spending was in this so-called catastrophic phase, when enrollees pay nothing for covered drugs and taxpayers and private Medicare plans pick up the cost.
  • Seniors' use of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs factored in the rise, with beneficiaries hitting the cost cap for these drugs earlier in the year than they did in 2024. Program spending surged from just $300 million in 2024 to $2 billion last year.
  • But there was double-digit spending growth across multiple classes of drugs, with cancer and diabetes treatments accounting for the largest spending increases.

Policy experts say the findings are important because Medicare drug plans have limited ability to control spending once enrollees hit the patient cost cap and face no cost sharing.

  • "The IRA gave plans an incentive to control spending, but few tools to do so," said American Enterprise Institute senior fellow Benedic Ippolito. "There are ways to modify the program that retain strong financial protections for enrollees while allowing for more cost containment."
  • Some analysts contend that overall Medicare spending will grow faster than the economy expands. The Cato Institute points to Congressional Budget Office projections showing Medicare drugs, doctors' visits and outpatient services will account for 44% of the federal deficit over the next decade.
  • But shifting more costs back onto seniors or cutting benefits could exacerbate health affordability concerns that already are leading some to skip medications and are driving up medical debt.

Between the lines: Predicting Medicare drug spending has always been tricky because it involves factoring an aging population, shifting costs and demand from seniors, and new laws like the IRA.

  • The increased use of specialty drugs has made drug expenses rise faster than other categories of medical spending.
  • Some of that has been offset by the use of lower-cost generics. And Medicare drug price negotiations starting this year are lowering the cost of some of the priciest brand-name medicines at the point of sale.
  • But Medicare trustees still project Part D drug costs will total about $222 billion this year, compared with $181 billion in 2025. By 2035, they're estimated to reach $346 billion.

What's next: The expiration of some provisions will likely shift more costs back on seniors.

  • A Biden-era program to stabilize insurance premiums will expire at the end of this year, meaning beneficiaries who buy stand-alone Medicare drug plans will pay more in January. The controversial program offers federal subsidies to insurers to keep patient monthly costs lower.
  • Further down the road, a 6% cap on annual increases in the Part D base premium expires in 2030. Subsidies now effectively absorb any difference.
  • Ippolito said Congress will have to reconsider the way the Medicare drug program is designed to control future spending, adding that extending current subsidy levels could easily cost over $100 billion for 10 years.

Options for another drug coverage overhaul include charging enrollees copays for certain higher-priced drugs after they exceed the cap — or changing how the patient cap is calculated.

  • Ippolito said Congress also could allow Medicare drug plans to slowly raise premiums to more historically normal levels so taxpayers and seniors share program costs more evenly.

The bottom line: Even those kinds of changes may not solve the cost problem, meaning policymakers will need to consider basic questions like how much to spend on Medicare drugs.

item.title: Labs are begging for someone to slow the AI race
item.description:
AI leaders are sounding the alarm as their own breakthroughs sharpen an extraordinary dilemma: slow down and risk falling behind, or press ahead and risk losing control.

Why it matters: AI executives and researchers increasingly see a race they can't safely slow on their own. Instead, they're urging governments, rivals and outside institutions to impose restraint across the field.

  • "The idea of racing forward at all costs seems absurd once one internalizes the seriousness of the stakes," OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki wrote Sunday.

Meanwhile, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said Tuesday he was leaving the company rather than contribute to what he sees as a race between OpenAI and Anthropic to build systems that will be difficult if not impossible to control.

  • "Neither company is acting responsibly," he said in a post on X. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
  • Colleague Evan Hubinger, who leads alignment science at Anthropic, posted in support of Coxon: "Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is (greater than) 10% within the next decade," he said. "I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to."

State of play: OpenAI has spent the past week unveiling capabilities so dramatic that its own leaders — and industry titans like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — openly invoked the arrival of artificial general intelligence, or AGI.

  • OpenAI defines the term as AI that can outperform humans across most economically valuable work.
  • GPT-6 Astra, released Thursday and heralded as a "generational leap" toward AGI, demonstrated major gains across science, coding, cybersecurity and professional work.

Zoom out: That burst of progress is fueling an existential debate inside OpenAI over how far — and how fast — the AI race can safely go.

  • "Currently I believe that no lab has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer," Pachocki wrote in a blog post titled "An Alien Mind."
  • Those fears turned concrete last month, when OpenAI agents escaped their intended environment and compromised Hugging Face — prompting the company to pause parts of its frontier-model development.

In a personal essay, OpenAI's head of strategic futures Dean Ball sketched out an even more unsettling possibility: "self-sovereign" AI agents operating beyond human control.

  • Such agents could earn money, buy their own computing power and spread across networks, forming what Ball likens to "autonomous digital corporations, or even societies."
  • "A genuine loss of control event is entirely possible if we do not act," Ball wrote.
OpenAI president Greg Brockman comments on Pachocki's essay. Screenshot via X.

The intrigue: The Trump administration, which has largely resisted binding AI regulation, sees slowing down as a threat of its own.

  • "We can't pause. You can't, because the Chinese won't pause," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday. "If they were to pull ahead of us on AI, then nothing else matters."

Between the lines: AI is beginning to accelerate its own development, shrinking the distance between one breakthrough and the next.

  • OpenAI said Sunday that it had reached its goal of creating an "automated research intern," but raised serious unresolved safety questions around AI systems that can help build increasingly powerful successors.
  • Two days later, OpenAI revealed that an unreleased model more powerful than Astra had produced a proof for one of mathematics' seven Millennium Prize problems — a historic breakthrough.

Reality check: AI labs have spent years warning that their technology could become extraordinarily dangerous, even as the business of building it has grown enormously lucrative.

  • "There is a long history of tech companies messaging one thing and then paying their lobbyists (internal & external) and trade associations to do the very opposite," New York Assemblymember Alex Bores posted on X.
  • Bores, an influential AI critic, pointed to OpenAI's efforts to weaken or defeat proposals for mandatory third-party audits in states including Massachusetts.

The other side: OpenAI says it's working on safeguards governments have yet to require, including a formal policy for publicly reporting serious AI incidents.

  • "My preferred policy is to have one. Right now we don't have one, and that's the big issue. And we're not alone in this," Ball told Axios.

The bottom line: The calls are coming from inside the house — from the people with the clearest view of how fast AI is advancing, and the strongest incentives to keep the race going.

  • "A genuine loss of control event is entirely possible if we do not act," Ball wrote.

  • "My preferred policy is to have one. Right now we don't have one, and that's the big issue. And we're not alone in this," Ball told Axios.

item.title: Historic NYT v. OpenAI copyright battle heats up
item.description:
A landmark copyright lawsuit filed by the New York Times against OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 moved into a critical new phase Friday, as all three parties presented their official arguments to a judge, with hopes of a favorable ruling ahead of a possible trial.

Why it matters: A ruling in favor of the Times could wreak havoc on the lucrative business models underpinning the AI industry.

  • A ruling in favor of OpenAI and Microsoft would serve as a massive blow to the publishing industry, potentially undermining its ability to control and monetize how content is scraped and used by AI giants.

Zoom in: In its motion for summary judgment, the Times argued OpenAI and Microsoft copied its works at scale to build commercial substitutes, which it believes violates the law.

  • OpenAI argued existing copyright laws and legal precedents allow tech giants to scrape publicly available works to train their large language models, and that reported facts are not protected by copyright law.
  • It cited studies that suggest outputs to queries via ChatGPT do not create commercial substitutes of the Times' work. Microsoft made similar claims for its Copilot AI product.

How it works: In its filing, OpenAI cites two recent California federal court decisions, Kadrey v. Meta and Bartz v. Anthropic, which found using copyrighted works to train AI models constituted as "fair use" in both of those cases because the training was considered transformative.

  • The Times doesn't dispute those findings, but says those cases are different and can't be applied to this suit because those plaintiffs didn't show that AI outputs competed with their products, creating market substitutions for their journalism.
  • The Times also argues that the case, which it filed in a New York federal court, should be evaluated against binding copyright precedents established by higher courts — the Supreme Court and the Second Circuit — rather than those recent lower court rulings.

Zoom out: Around the world, the case is being closely watched as a groundbreaking legal precedent that could shape the future of the AI industry.

  • This is especially true for the Trump administration, which has publicly tied its national security and economic goals to the development of AI infrastructure.
  • On Thursday, the Justice Department filed a brief supporting OpenAI in the case, arguing training large language models from millions of digital works delivers a transformative public benefit that offsets any competitive harm to the publishing industry.

What to watch: District Judge Sidney Stein is expected to rule in the coming months whether the case, or key portions of it, should move to trial next year.

item.title: LIV Golf files for bankruptcy protection
item.description:
LIV Golf — the Saudi-backed league that upended the sport with a costly splash but failed to identify a viable business model — filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on Tuesday.

Why it matters: It's an ignominious turn of events for a brash organization that lured some of the biggest stars away from the PGA Tour with enormous paydays that proved to be unsustainable.

The big picture: LIV represents a high-profile flop for its Saudi investors.

  • The bankruptcy filing comes after months of efforts to lure new backers and chart a new path for a league that struggled to draw significant TV ratings.

Catch up quick: The Public Investment Fund — Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund — confirmed in April that it was withdrawing support for the league after the 2026 season.

  • PIF — which ultimately plunged more than $5 billion into LIV, according to Money in Sport — decided to ditch LIV after President Trump's war in Iran scrambled geopolitics in the Middle East and jolted energy prices.
  • The fund said in a statement that the "substantial investment required by LIV Golf over a longer term is no longer consistent with the current phase of PIF's investment strategy."

Between the lines: LIV said Tuesday that it had secured a restructuring support agreement from an arm of BC Partners to reorganize operations and emerge "majority owned by players."

  • The bankruptcy could lead to the severing of key contracts, including with star players like Jon Rahm, whose defection to LIV was considered a significant loss for the PGA Tour.
  • It could also serve as a major turning point in the career of superstar Bryson DeChambeau, one of the initial players to leave the PGA for LIV.
  • PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp has made it clear that any players who want to return will need to earn their way back, calling the tour a meritocracy by its nature.
  • LIV said Tuesday that it "remains in advanced discussions with" the players.

Friction point: Critics of LIV and the players who joined it said the league amounted to "sportswashing" as the Saudis sought to redirect attention from human rights abuses.

  • Defenders — including LIV member and former PGA superstar Phil Mickelson — said the league would help grow the game on a global scale.

item.title: AI agents are poised to be the next hacking victims, cyber CEO predicts
item.description:
In a world of AI-enabled cyberattacks, the victims of hacks will no longer just be humans — they'll also be AI agents themselves, Bugcrowd CEO Dave Gerry told Axios.

Why it matters: Cyber defenses are tailored toward predicting and defending humans. Now, companies need to start treating the agents roaming their systems as both potential adversaries and the targets.

Driving the news: Gerry's prediction during an interview at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference last month came after OpenAI disclosed that its agentic system hacked Hugging Face but before the AI lab released its technical deep dive into how its agents carried out that attack.

What he's saying: "We're going to see agents as the victim," Gerry told Axios. "You're going to start to see agents getting hacked, not people."

The big picture: Gerry's prediction comes as AI labs continue to grapple with the long-tail impact of their agents taking unauthorized actions during pre-deployment security testing.

  • But many of those cases involve AI agents acting in unintended ways, not hacking each other as a way to break into an organization.

Zoom in: Gerry fully anticipates that the growing number of hacks against AI agents are going to take place in the enterprise, rather than on consumer-owned and operated agents, since that's where the bulk of AI agents are currently deployed.

  • "It's going to become the No. 1 attack vector that we're going to see," he said. "To make our lives easier as humans, we've given [AI agents] the crown jewels to everything."
  • He noted that many tools that companies have long relied on now also have agents themselves, making it harder to keep track of what's on a company network.
  • "You have all of these enterprise-approved tools that now magically got AI turned on," he said. "Now, there's a backlog of all of this tech debt of things that I approved that I no longer approve."

Between the lines: The cybersecurity industry has been trying to raise awareness about securing AI agents' identities for more than a year, warning that AI agents are now the latest example of insider threats.

  • Those insider agents could be leveraged to provide hackers with unfettered access to sensitive systems, exfiltrate data and break into other parts of an organization.
  • "To me, that's inevitable," Gerry said.

Zoom out: Even before AI agents started to proliferate in enterprise networks, poor identity controls were one of the top vectors for malicious hackers.

  • Identity-based cyberattacks accounted for 60% of all of Cisco's incident response cases in 2024, for example.

The intrigue: Visibility of the actions that AI agents are taking and their chain of thought is becoming more obfuscated as frontier models advance, making it more difficult for security teams to attribute attacks.

What we're watching: "It's new attacks. It's moving faster. It's moving at a bigger scale," Gerry said.

  • "But ultimately, this comes back to good cyber hygiene and understanding what exists and how do you put controls around it."

Go deeper: AI models are becoming unknowable

item.title: OpenAI's historic math solution overshadowed by credit controversy
item.description:
OpenAI says its AI has solved the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem, a potentially historic breakthrough shadowed by questions over unpublished research by outside mathematicians.

Why it matters: The controversy strikes at a core trust question for AI-assisted science: whether researchers can safely use frontier labs' tools to work on unpublished discoveries.

State of play: OpenAI said Tuesday an internal model "significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra" produced a proof that the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations can develop a singularity in finite time.

  • The company says the effort began Sept. 1, after OpenAI researchers heard rumors that two Millennium Prize problems had been solved and launched its new internal model at the remaining problems.
  • On a call with reporters, OpenAI executives said they devoted enormous computing power to the effort, putting the cost of solving the problem in the "millions of dollars" with roughly 10,000 agents at work.
  • The equation helps explain how fluids move, which could be used to better understand everything from blood circulation to weather patterns.

Friction point: NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge had been working on closely related fluid-dynamics research.

  • Buckmaster publicly questioned whether OpenAI raced down a research direction it learned about from their work and raised concerns about whether private Codex material could have played a role.
  • He also alleged that OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck pushed to remove Alpöge from authorship because he works for Anthropic, OpenAI's biggest competitor.
  • Buckmaster said that when he threatened to make their interactions public, Bubeck allegedly responded: "Why would you ruin your career?"

Between the lines: The controversy raises thorny questions about who owns the work completed with AI tools, and whether the labs are competing with their own customers.

Zoom in: OpenAI says it did not access Buckmaster or Alpöge's specific user data while pursuing the proof. But the company acknowledged Tuesday that it can't entirely rule out an indirect connection.

  • "While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models," OpenAI said.
  • By default, OpenAI says it doesn't train on inputs or outputs from enterprise customers. Users of personal ChatGPT accounts can opt out of having their conversations used for training.

What they're saying: "Now that we can see their work, the approaches appear to be different," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote on X.

  • Altman admitted OpenAI launched the effort after hearing rumors that Anthropic's models had solved a major math problem: "We were curious if ours could do it too."
  • OpenAI says it does not intend to claim the $1 million Millennium Prize, instead framing the result as evidence of how quickly its most advanced systems are improving.

Mady's thought bubble: It's striking that OpenAI spent millions of dollars in compute chasing a math breakthrough after hearing that outside researchers — including an Anthropic employee — were close to one themselves.

  • The episode raises an uncomfortable question: What happens when the company providing scientists with AI research tools can also mobilize vastly more resources to compete with them?

The bottom line: Disputes over what AI companies know about your work and usage of their tools are just beginning.

item.title: NYC unveils records suggesting officials knew air was unsafe after 9/11
item.description:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration released more than 170,000 pages of documents Tuesday that suggest city officials knew air conditions following the 9/11 attacks were unsafe, despite assurances otherwise.

The big picture: Twenty-five years later, New Yorkers are still seeking a full accounting of what city officials knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero and whether they were honest with the public about the risks.

  • More New York City Fire Department members have died of 9/11-related illnesses than the 343 killed in the attacks.
  • "It would be one thing if government had stood alongside survivors and provided them with everything they needed at every step of the way, and yet we know that could not be further from what actually happened," Mamdani said during Tuesday remarks.
  • "People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air."

Driving the news: The release includes air quality reports, contamination records and internal correspondence that shed light on what city officials knew about the toxic air near Ground Zero.

  • The public portal where the memos are stored was a more than $34 million commitment from City Hall, Mamdani said.
  • The released followed a settlement struck between Mamdani's administration and advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which has waged a long fight for transparency.

9/11 Health Watch executive director Ben Chevat said Tuesday that "since 9/11, four different mayoral administrations worked to keep the answer from the public, even as city officials at the time continued to say that the air was quote 'safe and acceptable.'"

  • The portal hosts what was found in 68 boxes of toxin-related documents uncovered by City Hall officials last year and archives from former Mayor Rudy Giuliani's office, like the so-called Harding Memo that predicted lawsuits related to toxic exposure, among other records.
  • Mamdani said that the city would continue to update the portal and, as part of the settlement, would appoint designated personnel to coordinate document gathering to help individuals obtain victim health benefits.
  • Since its 2011 reopening, the federally funded 9/11 Victim Compensation Fund has awarded more than $16.8 billion to over 71,000 claimants, per its most recent annual report.

Flashback: Christine Todd Whitman, the former head of the Environmental Protection Agency under the Bush administration, told The Guardian 10 years ago that she was wrong to assure New Yorkers that the air was safe.

What they're saying: Comedian Jon Stewart, who in the years following the attack became a vocal advocate for first responders' health, said at Tuesday's announcement that the city "buried" evidence for 25 years, starting soon after the attacks.

  • He put it bluntly: "The city began covering their ass three weeks in."

Go deeper: Accused 9/11 plotters to stand trial in 2028

item.title: The body image battle is real in 2026, but the bodies may not be
item.description:
A societal spotlight on extreme thinness is stripping body diversity from screens, just as fashion magazines did in the early aughts, mental health experts tell Axios.

The big picture: Fake content creators are introducing unattainable, AI-generated body images that prey on human nature and exacerbate the struggle for many to reach self-acceptance for their bodies.

  • When shrunken celebrities "become the ideal ... because of their status, then the virtual influencers are going to be emulating that," Katy Bruchmann, who leads Santa Clara University's Social Cognition and Comparison Lab, says.
  • "Then, the more really thin, super beautiful virtual influencers you have, the target changes for all the real people again. It's a really scary cycle."

Driving the news: Some are posing as influencers selling wellness products or services, while others are sharing body transitions or beauty advice.

  • Axios reviewed dozens of social media posts that include clear AI-generated body transformations or fitness influencers, while online sleuths have uncovered content that appears fake.

Zoom in: Some were labeled as AI. Many were not. But research from Brooke Bennett, the director of the Body image, Eating, Access, and Media Lab at the University of Clemson, and her colleagues found that it essentially doesn't matter.

  • Even when people know the image they're viewing is AI, it still hurts their body satisfaction.
  • "I think it's this expectation management piece," Bennett says. "We might... say, 'OK, I know that person's AI, but that doesn't mean that everyone else knows, and people are going to expect me to look like that too.'"

Zoom out: The striving for thinness has been fueled by a GLP-1 boom and pushed to extremes with dangerous internet trends. While "SkinnyTok" was banned by TikTok, the messages are still slipping through.

  • Coupled with images of flawless women wearing a size 00, social media can be a body image minefield.
  • "In the clinical space, we're seeing patients coming in really struggling to deal with some of this AI and ... social media pressures in general," Bennett says.

Follow the money: Tech and media companies have flooded the zone with a host of cyber stars that are accessible and low-cost.

  • "You can hire an AI influencer for cheap, and they can be in Brazil tonight selling a beverage, and in Tokyo tomorrow selling a T-shirt," Bruchmann says.

Our thought bubble: Beyond the completely virtual vixens, it's easier than ever to edit images using AI.

  • I tried it myself, asking ChatGPT to slim me down. I still looked like myself, with no immediate signs that the photo had been altered, like garbled text or extra fingers.

The fine print: When organic AI content is posted to Meta products, users can opt in to identify it, or Meta's system may.

  • TikTok "encourage[s]" creators to label content generated or significantly edited by AI. The platform may also label it.
  • But the rules aren't foolproof, and likely AI-generated content still appears unlabeled.

item.title: How extreme heat is rewriting the job of state government
item.description:
As climate change makes extreme heat more frequent and dangerous, states are building systems to manage a hazard they weren't historically built to handle.

The big picture: In a growing number of states, officials are appointing heat officers, writing statewide plans, setting worker protections, funding cooling infrastructure, and coordinating responses across agencies.

Driving the news: July was the hottest month ever measured in the contiguous U.S., with every Lower 48 state above its 20th-century average.

  • The speed at which states have ramped up their response to extreme heat has been "stunning," V. Kelly Turner, associate director of heat research at the UCLA Luskin Center for Innovation, told Axios.
  • "Heat's everywhere, but it's sort of fallen through the cracks," said Turner, a professor of urban planning at UCLA. "If everyone's responsible, no one's responsible."

Part of the problem, she said, is that heat historically hasn't carried the same obvious property damage price tag as disasters such as floods and wildfires, so it can attract less government funding.

  • "Heat's already competing with all these other climate problems, and it doesn't have its own home; it doesn't have its own budget," she said.

Context: Massachusetts announced in August that it became the first East Coast state and second in the nation after Arizona to appoint a heat resilience officer.

  • The state has warmed by nearly 3.5°F in the past century.
  • Massachusetts Department of Public Health data shows there were nearly 1,500 heat-related emergency room visits last year.
  • Heat resilience officer Katie Schlick told Axios that 1 in 5 Massachusetts public schools lacks air conditioning. Sending kids home affects their learning, she said.

State of play: Arizona's 2024 heat plan created its chief heat officer role to coordinate heat-response efforts across agencies. It also expanded heat-relief resources and deployed mobile solar-powered cooling centers made from shipping containers.

  • Visits to two cooling centers at the Arizona Capitol rose 59% in summer 2025 from a year earlier, according to the state.

California has no official with such a title, but Turner said "we do have an office that is dedicated to extreme heat and a dedicated funding program that's putting a lot of money into the hands of communities to work on the problem."

  • California's 2022 Extreme Heat Action Plan established what officials called the state's first "all-of-government framework" for extreme heat.
  • Its updated 2026 plan spans public health, emergency response, housing, infrastructure, energy and worker protections.
  • A separate law will require cities and counties to address extreme heat hazards when they next update certain general plan elements on or after Jan. 1, 2028. Turner said that ultimately means "every single community" will have a clause "that says here's how we're addressing heat."

What we're watching: Schlick's initial goals for Massachusetts include reducing heat-related school closures through more cooling, building local heat-planning capacity, creating safer workplaces, and planting more trees.

  • The state has identified "heat equity communities" where less tree cover, shade and green space leave residents particularly exposed, Schlick said.

Schlick doesn't know whether she'll have dedicated funding for heat initiatives and expects to draw on broader resilience investments and existing programs and partnerships.

  • She wants to better quantify heat's costs — including lost work and wages, ER visits, and insurance costs — and measure which interventions are cost-effective.

The bottom line: "It's very early days in terms of heat governance," Turner said, as states figure out what an effective response looks like.

item.title: The grocery aisle's new double whammy: price and safety
item.description:
Plenty of Americans feel like they're forking over a fortune for groceries—only to get hit with a recall notice that forces them to throw that expensive food out.

Why it matters: While grocery prices are driven by complex trade and energy costs, the safety net meant to keep them safe to eat is fraying, creating a dual crisis of affordability and safety.

  • The average American household pays more than $10,000 on groceries every year, and two-thirds of Americans think they're spending too much.
  • Prices have increased by more than 18% since 2022, although some foods have seen sharper or smaller increases.

What they're saying: "It can be really, really scary out there," Lauren Borsheim, a food policy analyst at Food & Water Watch, tells Axios.

  • "The Trump administration since 2025 has really just dismantled many of the fundamental protections we need to keep our food supply safe."
  • "We have people that are really afraid that the U.S. is not doing a good job regulating our food supply. It's definitely a concern out there that as people are spending more money on their food, they are also fearful that that same food is going to cause them to get sick," Borsheim says.

By the numbers: Recalls are relatively on par with normal levels this fiscal year, according to FDA data.

  • So far, 5,504 products have been recalled in 2026. That's up slightly from the 5,461 products recalled last year, but down from the 6,524 products recalled in 2024.

Yes, but: The FDA recently hit a record 19 simultaneous outbreak investigations, covering everything from infant formula to jalapeños.

Between the lines: Mega-corporations and corporate consolidation can turn single-suppliers' errors into multi-state panics, as seen with the Cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce.

  • "The U.S. food safety system has gotten hit so hard over the last year and a half," Christopher Barrett, an economist at Cornell University, tells Axios.

Zoom out: Food-safety advocates are concerned about declining federal surveillance after the Trump administration eliminated or pushed out thousands of workers across the CDC, FDA and USDA.

  • Those cuts prompted federal officials to say they plan to do fewer inspections.
  • Barrett says assuming staffing cuts won't affect food safety is "demonstrably false."
  • "When you cut corners, and you're not seeing the inspectors show up very often, then more stuff gets out the door. You get more episodes of foodborne illness. You have expensive recalls. That just adds to companies' costs, which gets turned into higher prices for us, and it's a vicious cycle," Barrett says.
  • The FDA did not respond to Axios' request for comment.

The other side: "The U.S. food supply remains one of the safest in the world," a USDA spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement.

  • The USDA "uses the best available science, data, inspection oversight, and technology to ensure standards do not slip, and to respond quickly when risks emerge."
  • "Inspectors and frontline personnel provide mandatory inspection coverage at every federally regulated establishment every day and that will not change," adding that no "regulated products can enter commerce without inspection."
  • "The number of recalls can fluctuate year to year for many reasons. Enhanced recordkeeping and traceability systems also help identify and remove affected products faster and more precisely, which can contribute to changes in recall totals over time."

The big picture: High-profile recalls are happening alongside persistent grocery inflation, but the two are not sharply connected, former USDA Chief Economist Joseph Glauber tells Axios.

  • Instead, the war in Iran is driving up energy prices, the president's trade policies and specific weather events are squeezing individual food categories, Glauber tells Axios.
  • Beef prices have risen amid low numbers of U.S. cattle and restrictions on Mexican cattle due to New World screwworm outbreaks, while tariffs have hit Mexican tomatoes and weather has struck the price of delicate fruits like citrus, Glauber says.

The bottom line: Inflation makes groceries hard to afford, but gutting federal watchdogs makes them hard to trust.

item.title: Iran war drives $100 billion in extra energy costs for U.S. consumers
item.description:
The war in Iran has now cost U.S. consumers $100 billion in higher energy prices, and the bill is rising another $1 million about every two minutes, per a real-time estimate from Brown University as of Monday morning.

Why it matters: Energy inflation shows up across the entire economy, and the recent surge in diesel prices in particular threatens to have a dramatic impact on freight and travel in the weeks and months to come.

By the numbers: The Iran War Energy Cost Tracker from Brown's Watson School says higher gasoline and diesel prices have cost the average U.S. household more than $760 since the war began Feb. 28.

  • Most of that is gas, though the diesel burden is rising faster of late.
  • On Friday, diesel hit an all-time record high, and it's continued to rise every day since. As of Monday morning it's at $5.90 a gallon, per AAA, up about 60% from a year ago.

Between the lines: Texas has borne the biggest share, with consumers paying around $11 billion in extra gas and diesel costs since the war began in late February, per the tracker.

  • California and Florida are next, at about $8 billion and $5 billion, respectively.

The big picture: President Trump insists Americans are willing to pay higher prices to keep Iran from having a nuclear weapon.

  • Yet voters consistently say inflation is their most important issue, and on that subject they give the president substantial negative marks.

What we're watching: There's still a great deal of uncertainty over how much oil is getting out of the Middle East, which will impact fuel prices in the coming weeks and months.

  • The war in Ukraine is also having a significant effect, as Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure move global markets, particularly for diesel.

The bottom line: Consumers are in for a longer period of higher fuel prices than anyone expected when the war began.

  • With less than two months until the midterm elections, it'll be hard to temper their anger.

item.title: Axios interview: Altman sees revenge of "idea guy"
item.description:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says this era is bringing the revenge of the "idea guy" — the once-annoying aspiring entrepreneur burbling about their brainstorm with no technical chops to pull it off.

  • Altman says it would be like saying: "I have a great idea for a song. I just need that guy with the guitar to make it for me."
  • "It really did strike me as ridiculous," Altman told me in Chapel Hill, N.C. "But now we're watching a whole generation of people iterate on ideas faster than they ever could. The economics have been reset for what it means to make a new small business or large business."

Why it matters: Polls show most Americans think the risks of AI outweigh the benefits, with data-center rage as a bipartisan bonfire in the midterms. Altman — who's trying to sell AI into a massive backlash — wants to remind Americans that amid all the real risks, AI can equal opportunity.

  • "This is gonna be the best time in the world to do a startup," Altman said recently.

Reality check: These new tools are great for idea people. But most people are doers, not dreamers, and don't feel they have the time or AI skills to spin up a startup in their spare time.

  • Our experience is that AI is a real unlock for a very small percentage of people who are idea generators or problem solvers, and in a position to put that into action.

By the numbers: An American startup boom ignited during COVID and continued through this summer. Filings of new-business applications have continued to set records in the chatbot era.

  • The number of new U.S. businesses formed in the first half of this year, over 3 million, is the most for a January-June stretch in Census Bureau data going back to 2005.

The backstory: I first heard Altman's "idea guy" riff last spring, when he was talking onstage with Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, who asked how traits of successful founders were changing in this era.

  • "We would make fun of these [idea] people," Altman said. "They weren't that successful. And it was kind of always personally annoying to me. All of a sudden it's like the revenge of the idea guys."
  • "For a long time, the most important ingredient ... in a founding team was technical talent, and that's still very important. But now people who just really deeply understand their users and can't code at all, I want to fund those people. And that's a big turnaround."

That stuck in my mind. So when I sat down with Altman, 41, last week at the Carolina Inn in a bilateral meeting room during the G20 Innovation Ministerial, I asked him how that notion could be useful for today's AI users, or for people who should be wielding AI but are skeptics.

  • With GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI's powerful new model, Altman said, "you can start and run a small business effectively. ... It's like anyone who wants to have a company now has genius-level employees in every area of expertise."

Zoom in: AI makes many ideas monetizable that never would have penciled out in the past. "I met this guy recently who had used [GPT-]5.6 to make a piece of software that he had sold to 50 people for, like, $500 a month ... He was so happy."

  • "This would have cost you millions of dollars if you had to pay for software engineers," Altman told me. "All of a sudden you had an idea, you had this tiny corner of this tiny industry, there's one particular kind of task, and you were able to get software written for it. And of course people will pay for that."
  • "With the new model [Astra], someone made a computer game ... probably only fun or funny to people that work at OpenAI. There is real economic value in this to a few thousand people. The economics of making a full computer game for a few thousand people never possibly made sense before. And now they do."

The bottom line: "Whether it's a little thing to make your own life more convenient or a big thing that can create a business that adds huge value to other people," Altman said, "the space of viability has increased dramatically."

item.title: A growing movement wants AI out of schools
item.description:
America's two largest school districts both imposed sweeping AI bans this past week, hitting the brakes on a technology that's rapidly making its way into classrooms around the country.

Why it matters: Research on AI's educational value is mixed. Some studies have found personalized AI tutors can improve learning, while other research has linked AI-assisted essay writing to weaker critical thinking.

Driving the news: New York City's public school district blocked AI use for roughly 600,000 students in Pre-K through 8th grade, restricting it to specific uses for high school students.

  • Hours later, Los Angeles Unified imposed a districtwide moratorium on AI use on school devices for the 2026-27 school year, following a separate screen-time crackdown.
  • And Chicago school board candidates are lining up to sign a pledge demanding a three-year moratorium on generative AI in its schools.

What they're saying: Nicki Petrossi, a mother and co-founder of the Tech-Safe Learning Coalition, tells Axios one parent called today's kids "the guinea pig generation," adding, "you won't find a parent who's not concerned about this."

  • Another parent told her that their "five-year-old, who still believes in the Tooth Fairy, [is] being asked to interact with chatbots. What could go wrong?"

Between the lines: Bans may be hard to enforce because AI is already embedded in classroom technology.

  • Google's Gemini, for example, can appear when students search on school Chromebooks.

item.title: Trump's energy boss wavers on gasoline price path
item.description:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Sunday cautiously predicted gasoline price relief is on the way, but stopped short of firm or precise pledges.

Why it matters: Pump prices are at their highest Labor Day weekend levels on record, and the midterms loom less than two months away.

  • His appearances on Sunday political shows also comes as diesel prices, which ripple through the economy, are at all-time highs.

"I think prices headed downward is — is not an unreasonable expectation," he said on CBS's "Face the Nation."

State of play: On that show and others, Wright noted that U.S. gasoline demand typically falls after Labor Day with the end of the traditional summer driving season.

  • He also promoted recent administration moves to ease some environmental requirements for summer gasoline blends.
  • "Gasoline production is about to go up and demand is about to go down. So, if I had to guess, they're more likely to go down than go up," Wright said on CNN's "State of the Union."

Catch up quick: U.S. regular gasoline prices averaged $4.15 per gallon Sunday, per AAA data.

Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios

The intrigue: Wright also pointed to declining prices for gasoline futures contracts in the months ahead.

  • "The marketplace thinks gasoline prices are going to move meaningfully lower. So trust the market, certainly don't trust my predictions.," he said on ABC's "This Week," per a transcript.

Yes, but: Futures prices months ahead are volatile, and they're not a crystal ball for what will be happening in retail markets.

  • Pump prices have climbed in recent weeks amid a flare-up in hostilities that has driven crude oil prices higher.
  • Crude oil is already at its highest level in roughly six weeks, with the global benchmark above $96 per barrel at Friday's close, even though more oil appears to have been transiting the Strait of Hormuz recently.

What we're watching: Oil prices could see another jump when markets open for the week, following fresh conflicts this weekend.

item.title: Republicans sour on the economy
item.description:
Republicans' confidence in the economy has plummeted over the last six months at a pace unseen since Covid — reminiscent of the declines during the global financial crisis nearly two decades ago.

Why it matters: Usually, the president's party is upbeat about the economy, while the party out of power is far more downcast. What's striking now is that Republicans have grown increasingly sour this year, even with a Republican president in office.

  • It's another in a long list of ominous indicators for President Trump heading into the final two months before Election Day.

By the numbers: Since February, Republican consumer sentiment has plunged 15.1 index points, from 97.1 to 82, according to the latest University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers data. Democratic sentiment has fallen just 1.6 index points, from 41.8 to 40.2.

  • The 82 reading is lower than at any point during either of Trump's presidencies, with one exception: December 2020, after he had lost reelection but before he left office.
Data: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers; Chart: Mike Zapler/Axios

Flashback: It's rare for one party's outlook to remain steady while the other's falls — typically they move in tandem. But a similar split occurred during the global financial crisis in late 2008 and early 2009.

Caveat: That period included the election and inauguration of a Democratic president, accounting for some of the Republican decline.

What they're saying: "The vast majority of the time, Republicans and Democrats move broadly in parallel," Joanne Hsu, director of the Surveys of Consumers, told Axios. But that is not the case now.

  • "Republicans were expecting very positive results from administration policies" on the economy, including tariffs, she added. "But they haven't seen a slowdown in inflation, let alone" the reduction in prices that Trump promised.

Yes, but: Hsu said it's important to remember that, despite the slide, Republicans still have a much more positive outlook on the economy than Democrats.

  • For instance, Republicans still broadly believe gas prices will fall once the Iran war is over, which is not the case with Democrats, she said.

Zoom in: The Michigan survey tracks with other data on how Republicans feel about the economy under Trump, including a July Pew Research poll.

  • Forty-one percent of Republicans or Republican-leaning independents called the economy excellent or good — down 8 percentage points from January.
  • And the share of Republicans who said Trump's policies have made the economy worse rose from 18 percent to 28 percent. The share who said the policies have improved conditions dropped from 57 percent to 42 percent.

The other side: "The hard data of consumer spending and retail sales have, for months, consistently reinforced that the American consumer remains resilient thanks to the President's proven economic agenda of tax cuts and deregulation," said White House spokesman Kush Desai.

  • "As the Administration's economic policies, trade deals, and trillions in investments continue to materialize, Americans can count on more progress to come," he added.

The bottom line: It's no secret that the election will turn on the economy. Inflation remains untamed, and the war in Iran shows no sign of ending.

  • Trump has always been able to rely on bedrock support from Republicans, but even that is starting to crack.
